title: Time and Space Complexity
summary: Elementary operations, RAM model, line-by-line counting, T(n) efficiency function, simple loops, nested loops, mixed for + while loops and space complexity.

learningObjectives.text: Understand what resources algorithm analysis measures.
Distinguish between analyzing an algorithm and analyzing an implementation.

terms.label: Algorithm analysis
terms.definition: Study of how algorithms behave in terms of resources consumed, mainly time and space.

terms.label: Time complexity
terms.definition: Number of operations that an algorithm executes depending on the size of input n.

terms.label: Space complexity
terms.definition: Additional memory required by an algorithm, considering local variables, parameters and data structures.

terms.label: OE
terms.definition: Elementary operation. Operation whose cost is considered constant within the RAM model.

terms.label: RAM Model
terms.definition: Random Access Machine. Abstract model used to count elementary operations independently of a specific machine.

terms.label: T(n)
terms.definition: Time efficiency function of the algorithm as a function of the size of input n.

chapters.title: Time and Space Complexity
chapters.summary: Initial module of the course: introduces resource analysis, counting elementary operations and the construction of T(n).

learningObjectives.text: Understand the general purpose of algorithm analysis.
Recognize that time and space are the main resources.

content.text: Algorithm analysis studies how algorithms behave in terms of the resources they consume: mainly time (execution speed) and space (used memory). The objective is to be able to compare algorithms independently of the machine or the programmer that implements them.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish implementation algorithm.
Understand why multiplicative constants do not define the order of growth.

content.text: If two programmers N and D implement the same algorithm differently, both implementations will have the same growth order. The difference between them will be, at most, a multiplicative constant:
This means that two implementations of the same algorithm only differ by a constant factor. Therefore, when we talk about efficiency, we separate the algorithm from its implementation.
You always have to analyze the algorithm, not the program. The programming language and programmer's style affect the constants, but not the order of growth.

learningObjectives.text: Define time complexity.
Recognize elementary operations according to the RAM model.
Understand the basic pseudocode structure used in the course.

content.text: Time complexity measures how many operations an algorithm executes based on the size of input n. It is calculated by counting, line by line, how many times each instruction is executed and at what cost.
What are Elementary Operations (OE)?
They are operations whose cost is considered proportionally stable for the analysis. The RAM (Random Access Machine) model defines what they are:

blocks.title: Elementary operations according to the RAM model

content.text: The ends (endfor, endwhile, endif) are not counted as operations. The body of a loop is always executed one less time than the header.
Structure of an algorithm (pseudocode)
An algorithm in pseudocode has the following structure:

sections.title: 1.3 Example 1 - Algorithm with a for loop (Mindless Algorithm)

learningObjectives.text: Count the cost of a simple for loop.
Empirically verify linear growth.
Construct T(n) by adding costs per line.

content.text: Determine the efficiency function T(n) of the following algorithm.
Pseudocode

blocks.title: AlgorithmSM
blocks.code:
int AlgorithmSM (I int n) {
 int i, sum
 sum <- 0          # 1 time --> 1 * C1
 for i <- 1 to n do      # n+1 times --> (n+1) * C2
  sum <- sum + i       # n times --> n * C3
 endfor
 return sum         # 1 time --> 1 * C4
}

content.text: 1 Line by line tracking

blocks.title: Line-by-line tracing of the algorithm with a for loop

content.text: Why does the for have 3 OE? Because in each pass three things happen: the comparison i <= n is evaluated, at the end of the body i <- i+1 is incremented and the first time the assignment i <- 1 is made. That's why the header costs 3 OE per pass.

The body of a for loop is always executed one less time than the header: if the header goes n+1 times, the body goes n times. The last pass of the header is the one that fails the condition and does not execute the body.
2 Tabulating analysis (empirical verification)
We run the algorithm mentally for small values of n and count how many EOs occur. This gives us an idea of ​​how T(n) grows before calculating it formally.

blocks.title: Empirical verification for small values of n

content.text: Observe that when n increases by 1, T(n) always increases by 5. This confirms that the growth is linear: each additional unit of n always costs the same.
If the difference between consecutive rows of T(n) is constant, the function is linear. If the difference grows linearly, it is quadratic. If it grows exponentially, it is exponential.
3 Summation technique to obtain T(n)
This algorithm does not require complex summations because each line is executed a fixed number of times. We simply add the costs of all the lines:

steps.title: Sum of costs
steps.latex: T(n) = 1 \cdot C_1 + (n+1) \cdot C_2 + n \cdot C_3 + 1 \cdot C_4

content.text: Where a = C2 + C3 and b = C1 + C2 + C4 are positive constants. The result is a linear function in n.

learningObjectives.text: Analyze two nested for loops with fixed limit.
Recognize quadratic growth.
Construct T(n) for n-by-n nesting.

content.text: Determine the efficiency function of two nested for loops where both go from 1 to n (fixed limit).
Pseudocode

blocks.title: AlgorithmSM2 with fixed limits
blocks.code:
AlgorithmSM2 (I int A[n]) {
 x <- 1            # 1 time --> 1*1
 for i <- 1 to n do      # n+1 times --> (n+1)*3
  for j <- 1 to n do     # n(n+1) times --> n(n+1)*3
   x <- x + i        # n*n times --> n^2 * 2
  endfor
 endfor
}

content.text: 1 Line by line tracking

blocks.title: Costs per line in nested loops with fixed limit

content.text: Why is the internal for executed n*(n+1) times? The external for has n+1 header passes. For each of those passes, the internal for also has n+1 passes of its own. But the outer body only occurs n times, so the inner for is started n times, and each start has n+1 header passes. Total: n * (n+1).

sections.title: 1.5 Example 3 - Nested For with variable limit

learningObjectives.text: Analyze a nested loop whose internal limit depends on the external index.
Recognize the pattern n(n+1)/2.
Use linearity of summations.

content.text: Now the internal loop goes from 1 to i (variable limit that depends on the external one). This is the most frequent case in the analysis of sorting algorithms.
Pseudocode

blocks.title: SM2 algorithm with variable limit
blocks.code:
AlgorithmSM2 (I int A[n]) {
 x <- 1            # 1 time
 for i <- 1 to n do      # n+1 times
  for j <- 1 to i do     # VARIABLE UPPER BOUND: depends on i
   x <- x + i
  endfor
 endfor
}

sections.title: 1.6 Example 4 - For with internal while (logarithmic growth)

learningObjectives.text: Analyze a for loop with internal while.
Understand why a multiplicative update produces logarithms.
Recognize Theta(n log n) growth.

content.text: This is the richest case: the inner loop is a while that doubles j, producing logarithmic behavior. It is the pattern that explains why algorithms such as binary search or Merge Sort are so efficient.
Pseudocode

blocks.title: AlgorithmXXX
blocks.code:
AlgorithmXXX (I int n) {
 x <- 1            # 1 time --> 1*1
 for i <- 1 to n do      # n+1 times --> (n+1)*3
  j <- 1           # n times --> n*1
  while (j <= n) do     # n*(log2(n)+2) times --> n*(log2(n)+2)*1
   j <- j*2         # n*(log2(n)+1) times --> n*(log2(n)+1)*2
  endwhile
 endfor
}

content.text: 1 Detailed trace - how many times is the while executed?
The key is to understand what j <- j*2 does. Each time you pass the while, j is doubled:
The while stops when j > n, that is, when 2^k > n. How many times does it double before exceeding n?
+1 because j starts at 1 (= 2^0), not at 2 (= 2^1). The first iteration does not advance towards n, it only establishes the initial position.
+1 because the while header is evaluated once more at the end: it is the evaluation that fails the condition and causes the exit.

content.text: Space complexity measures how much additional memory an algorithm requires. The local variables, parameters and data structures used are counted.
